catalog_quote: Other East Kainji languages have much reduced systems. For example, tiMap (=Amo), appears to have two tones plus a rising tone in the account of Anderson (1980). Shimizu (1979, 1982a) usually transcribes the tonal systems in his lists as High and Low or High, Low and Downstep and he reconstructs the latter for his 'Proto-North-Jos'. ... [Blench 2004 ms:] Anderson (1980) does not explicitly set out the tonology of tiMap but it appears to have two tones plus a rising tone in his account.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: both quoted passages are verbatim in the held Blench 2021 (PDF p.15, sec. 3.1) and Blench 2004 ms (PDF p.5) files; locators correct. (2) The deciding source is a 2021 peer-reviewed comparative survey of East Kainji whose tiMap tone statement is explicitly second-hand and hedged (Blench reading tone marks in Anderson 1980's noun-class paper); neither primary (Di Luzio 1972 grammar sketch with phonology section; Anderson 1980) is held or openly available. (3) Nothing found suggests the classification is wrong: WALS 13A (Maddieson, read from Di Luzio 1972 + Anderson 1980) independently codes Amo 'Simple tone system'; Blench 2018 (LangSci, downloaded) is silent; no source anywhere mentions word stress for Amo; all described East Kainji relatives are tonal. Hence 'tonal, no stress rule described' stands, but the evidence is second-hand -> status thin rather than at-risk. (4) Acti

sources.quote: None. The tiMap section treats noun-class prefixes and concord only ('The correct name for the language of the Map people is tiMap. Its noun classes are described [under the name Amo] in (Di Luzio 1972; Anderson 1980)...'); no tone inventory or stress/accent statement for tiMap. General remark p.63-64 area: 'Tone-marking in particular is somewhat impressionistic.'

sources.note: The only primary description of Amo with a phonology section (59 pp; Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description; source of UPSID 220 and WALS 13A 'simple tone system'); our tonal coding rests on Blench's second-hand, hedged reading of Anderson 1980. Its phonology chapter would state the tone inventory directly and show whether any stress/accent remark exists.
